name: faust
desc: Functional programming language for real time signal processing
why: A functional language for signal processing that compiles DSP code to many targets, a genuinely distinctive way to make sound.

brief.what_it_is: Faust (Functional Audio Stream) is a functional programming language for real-time audio signal processing and synthesis, built at GRAME in Lyon. You write DSP code in the Faust language, and the Faust compiler translates it into C++, C, LLVM IR, WebAssembly, Rust and other targets. Wrapper scripts called architectures then turn the generated code into plugins (VST, AU, LV2, CLAP and others), standalone apps, mobile or web apps, and objects for Max, Pure Data, SuperCollider and similar hosts. The README describes it as 'fully compiled', and the homepage calls it an alternative to C++ that is much simpler to learn.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames Faust as a way to design synthesizers, instruments and audio effects in a functional language, then ship the same DSP specification to many platforms without rewriting it by hand. It has been developed at GRAME since 2002.
brief.how_it_works: A Faust program is a DSP specification that the compiler translates to sample-level code for the chosen language. The master branch can emit LLVM IR and use an LLVM JIT, which lets libfaust be embedded in C++ programs and used by tools such as FaustLive. The faust2... scripts combine the generated code with a chosen architecture file (JACK, ALSA, Qt, VST, and so on) to produce a finished binary or plugin.

commands_seen.context: README example: compiles a Faust file into a JACK application with a Qt interface.
README tip: type faust2 in a terminal and press Tab to auto-complete and list every faust2... tool.
Maintainer-side: updates the libraries submodule to its latest version before committing it to the main repo. Not something a user needs to run.

brief.install_notes: Since release 2.5.18 the build and install is CMake-based. The README points to the GitHub wiki (BuildingSimple tutorial) for compiling from source. Official packages are on the GitHub releases page. Each faust2... script needs its own dependencies installed, for example faust2jaqt needs JACK and Qt. Faust libraries live in a separate repo included as a git submodule, so a source checkout needs submodules. No account or license key is mentioned. The browser tools (Faust Playground, Online Faust IDE) need no install.
brief.standout: Compile-to-everything from one functional DSP source is the core trick. Also notable: the Faust Web IDE and Playground run the compiler in the browser, so you can try a DSP program with no install, and the web tooling is a live part of the project, with 2026 news including a Godot integration and an experimental Rust port (faust-rs) that adds forward and reverse-mode automatic differentiation.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage news runs through September 2, 2026 (Google Summer of Code projects finalized). Three CI badges (Ubuntu, macOS, Windows) appear in the README. I did not check the GitHub commit date or the latest release tag, so this rests on the news and CI links.
brief.caveats: Each faust2... target has its own dependencies, so some will not build out of the box. The homepage flags faust-rs, the Rust port, as exploratory and not production-ready. The executable list is long and mostly thin wrappers, so most users will only need a few. The README does not state a license in what I read. The homepage has a small factual slip: it lists IFC-26 in Cannes as being in Italy.
quotes: Faust (Functional Audio Stream) is a functional programming language specifically designed for real-time signal processing and synthesis.
A distinctive characteristic of Faust is that it is fully compiled.
The fastest way to get an exhaustive list of all of them is to open a terminal window, type faust2, and then press the Tab key for auto-completion.
